source: Cao, Wang, Qin, Zhang, Xie (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling (arXiv listing, status check 2026-10-26)
finding: The arXiv page still lists only v1 (13 May 2026). No later version, no comments, no code link. The paper itself says the code, prompts and data are planned for future release. No independent replication was found as of today.
numbers: Submission history: v1 only, 13 May 2026. Page comments: none. Code links: none. The API record shows an 'updated' stamp of 2026-10-25, but the abs page lists no new version.
quote: future work, we plan to release the code, prompts, and data
limits: Absence of a listing is not proof that nobody replicated it privately. The web search quota ran out in this pass, so only the arXiv page, two citing papers and a few searches were checked.
agent_relevance: Treat the +8.6 as one team's unreplicated number. Plan our own replication, not a citation.

source: Cao, Wang, Qin, Zhang, Xie (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling (full text, ablation protocol and Table 2)
finding: Re-read of Table 2 and its notes. All ablations use one 100-question subset drawn from the test benchmarks, one solver (Sonnet 4.6), pass@1 44.0 and oracle@4 53.0. The word 'seed' does not appear anywhere in the text, so there is no seed-level variance. The random-retry arm has a very narrow CI [43,48] against about 20 points for every other arm, which suggests it is an average over repeated draws while the other arms are one run. Random retry reached an early-stop hit rate of 42.6 versus 76.7 for the learned controller at the same mean K of 2.58.
numbers: Full harness 47.0 [37,57], K 2.58. Random retry matched K 45.7 [43,48], K 2.58. JOL-only 45.0, FOK-only 42.0, hand rule (1-JOL)xFOK 42.0 at K 2.40. Last answer of 4: 40.0. Max-JOL of 4: 44.0. No prior state, K=4: 45.0. Full previous context: 40.0 at K 3.09. Bootstrap B=5,000 over 100 records.
limits: The CI mismatch means 47.0 vs 45.7 is not a like-for-like paired test. A gap of 1.3 points is far inside noise. A directed-vs-random difference can only be judged with per-item paired data on N of at least 500. The CI-width reading is my inference.
agent_relevance: Closes nothing; confirms gap 2 is open. Our own test must run both arms on the same items and report a paired bootstrap on per-item differences.

source: Cao, Wang, Qin, Zhang, Xie (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling (Table 1 panel B and Table 5)
finding: Re-read of the cost comparison. The pooled table has no plain best-of-2.4, no majority vote and no self-consistency arm. The only 4-attempt parallel methods are Verifier Reranking and Aggregator, both at K=4 and about 1.7x to 1.8x the harness cost. On LiveCodeBench the Aggregator is within 0.9 points of the harness at 1.7x cost, so the cost advantage is real but the accuracy edge over a simple parallel baseline is small on code.
numbers: Pooled (N=1,859): Pass@1 48.3 at $0.29; Self-Refine 52.4 at $0.45 (K 1.5); Budget forcing 51.5 at $0.67; Verifier 49.8 at $1.32 (K 4.0); Aggregator 53.7 at $1.42 (K 4.0); Harness 56.9 at $0.78 (K 2.4, oracle 62.2). LiveCodeBench v6 (N=388): Pass@1 74.3 at $0.24; Aggregator 83.4 at $0.94; Harness 84.3 at $0.56 (K 2.6, oracle 86.0). The Table 5 text layout was scrambled, so the row-to-method mapping there was inferred from the pooled table.
limits: The harness oracle (62.2 at K 2.4) is above the Aggregator oracle (60.5 at K 4.0). So the harness candidate set is better than four independent samples. That is odd for a method that only adds attempts on hard items. It may reflect compact feedback on retries, or that FOK is fed into the solve prompt. Not isolated by the paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open. A fair test needs plain best-of-K with majority vote at the harness's measured token total, per benchmark.

source: Cao, Wang, Qin, Zhang, Xie (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling (diagnosis card, Figure 3)
finding: The pass/fail rubric is AUROC at least 0.60 and ECE at most 0.15, on a 100-item anchor set. Two readings matter for us. First, ECE alone can pass a signal that carries little information: Gemma 4 passes the joint ECE row (0.044) while its FOK AUROC fails (0.534) and its joint AUROC is only 0.699. Second, a signal can rank well and still be badly miscalibrated before the SVM fix: Gemini 3 Flash FOK AUROC 0.818 but FOK ECE 0.465 and JOL ECE 0.528; its joint ECE after the SVM is 0.149, one thousandth under the bar.
numbers: Sonnet 4.6 (anchor accuracy 0.58): FOK AUROC 0.612 / ECE 0.132; JOL AUROC 0.745 / ECE 0.112; joint AUROC 0.757 / ECE 0.087. Gemini 3 Flash (accuracy 0.34): joint AUROC 0.834, joint ECE 0.149. Gemma 4 (accuracy 0.19): joint AUROC 0.699, joint ECE 0.044. All N=100.
limits: With N=100 the standard error of an AUROC near 0.6 is roughly 0.06 (rule of thumb, not computed in the paper), so 0.612 against a 0.60 bar is close to a coin flip. The paper gives no CI for these AUROC values.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: our gate should require an AUROC whose bootstrap lower bound is above 0.6, and should not accept ECE alone. The anchor size needed is still unknown.

source: Cao, Wang, Qin, Zhang, Xie (2026) LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling (Section H, limitations)
finding: The authors name their own limits: not model-universal, main evaluation only on Sonnet 4.6, controller fitted on a small anchor set that may limit robustness under distribution shift, benchmarks only, no long-horizon agent tests. This confirms gaps 4 and 9 from the authors' side.
numbers: Anchor set N=100, disjoint from the downstream benchmarks. Nine models were diagnosed; one (Sonnet 4.6) passed every row.
quote: controller is fitted on a small anchor set
limits: Self-reported limits; they do not report a test of how robust the controller is to anchor size.
agent_relevance: Do not claim transfer to agent tasks. Treat the harness as a design to test, not a result to import.

source: Dahal, Bakhtin, Cohen et al. (2026) Thinking Before Thinking: Scaling Agentic Inference Through Meta-Reasoning (Meta Superintelligence Labs)
finding: A separate controller-and-workers harness for long agentic runs (ProgramBench, IMO ProofBench, ARC-AGI-2, LongCoT-mini). It cites Cao et al. as related work on metacognitive signals, but it is not a replication: it does not use FOK or JOL, and it controls multi-step runs. It beats a matched 'Direct Control Agent' with the same workers and the same nominal model-call budget in all 12 matched comparisons, but loses at small budgets. The authors say they cannot attribute the gain to any component.
numbers: Budgets 100 calls (reasoning sets) and 1,200 calls (ProgramBench). ProgramBench: GPT-5.5 meta 71.5 vs direct 63.7 vs Codex 58.0; Opus 4.8 meta 67.2 vs direct 65.3 vs Claude Code 65.5. Opus at 400 calls: meta 56.6 vs direct 62.7 (loses). GPT-5.5 direct control uses about 18% of its 1,200-call allowance; meta uses 89% to 101%. IMO ProofBench has only 30 problems. Gains over direct control 3.6 to 4.2 points averaged over three models on the other benchmarks.
quote: equal call allowances do not imply equal token cost, latency, or FLOPs
limits: Matched on calls, not tokens, cost or FLOPs (the authors say so). Direct control stops early and leaves budget unused, so part of the gain is just more spend. No stage-removal, state-only or memory ablation. Not uncertainty-gated.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to an agent-scale result (gap 9), but it supports 'structured control and compact state beat a flat history at a large call budget', not 'confidence gates work'. The overhead at small budgets matters: a fixed monitoring cost must be repaid.

source: Liu, Gani, Lu, Thomas, Steyvers, Cohan (2026) Metacognition in LLMs: Foundations, Progress, and Opportunities
finding: A July 2026 survey (Yale, UC Irvine). It cites Cao et al. once, in the sentence that such judgments generally do not translate to reliable strategic adaptation [29], and does not treat the harness as a replicated result. It also notes that overconfidence led to poor decisions in agentic settings, and that task-difficulty prediction is hard out of distribution. This is the second of the two Semantic Scholar citers named in the critique, and it is a survey, not a replication.
numbers: Survey text; no new experiments. The harness paper is reference [29].
quote: does not translate to reliable strategic adaptation
limits: I read the cited sentence and the agentic and monitoring sections, not the whole survey.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: both known citers are now read (this survey and the Meta paper d06); neither replicates. A citation is not a replication.

source: Tsui (2026, COLM) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Large Language Models (arXiv v3, 2 Aug 2026)
finding: The same error is injected as the model's own output or attributed to the user. 14 open non-reasoning models fix the user's error but not their own. Reasoning models show a small, even negative, blind spot, so they do correct errors that sit in their own context. This is not the Huang protocol (no 'review your answer' prompt on a finished answer), but it is the best 2026 test of whether a model acts on its own mistakes. Appending 'Wait' to a base model nearly matches its reasoning sibling.
numbers: Average blind spot 64.5% over 14 models; 62.8% on logic and tracking tasks; Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Claude Sonnet 4 41.4%. 'Wait' cuts the blind spot by 89.3%. DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.567 -> 0.902 with 'Wait' vs DeepSeek-R1-0528 0.908; Qwen3-14B 0.117 -> 0.868 vs reasoning mode 0.843. 5,306 error-correction fine-tuning traces cut the blind spot by 76.0%.
quote: Appending Wait requires no training yet reduces the blind spot by 89.3%
limits: Injected errors are short and synthetic; no Sonnet 4.6 or other 2026 frontier reasoning model measured; open models dominate. Measures whether the model corrects in-context errors, not whether a separate review prompt helps on a finished answer.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: reasoning-trained models do self-correct inside a trace, and the fix for non-reasoning models is cheap. Guardrail G1 (no prompted self-critique without evidence) should be scoped to non-reasoning or short-trace settings until we test it on our own model.

source: Tie et al. (2025) Can LLMs Correct Themselves? A Benchmark of Self-Correction in LLMs (CorrectBench, arXiv v2 Oct 2025)
finding: A broad benchmark of intrinsic, external and fine-tuned correction on commonsense, math and code. Intrinsic methods help on average for instruction models, which is a softer result than Huang et al., but reasoning models (DeepSeek-V3, QwQ, o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1) gain little and pay a time cost. A plain CoT prompt is competitive on accuracy per token.
numbers: MATH cost table (150 samples): Base 68.5 at 791 tokens; CoT 69.5 at 1,804; CoVe 75.0 at 2,019; RCI 70.2 at 1,780 tokens and 1.2 calls; Reflexion-v1 72.8 at 3.5 calls; RATT 78.7 at 2,185 tokens and 3 calls. One instruct model's rows show deltas from -18.8 (CoVe) to +22.1 (RCI, one dataset); the table layout was scrambled so the model and column are not certain. DeepSeek-R1 base: GSM8K 92.63, MATH 84.21, GPQA 41.15.
quote: reasoning LLMs already incorporate robust intrinsic correction mechanisms
limits: Labels DeepSeek-V3 a 'reasoning LLM', which is a stretch. Several 'intrinsic' methods use few-shot templates or other scaffolding, so they are not the pure Huang protocol. No Claude 2026 model. Tokens are not matched across methods. The cost table has only 150 samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: no evidence that prompted revision adds value for reasoning models at its token price. It does not show the revision fails either; it shows a small, costly gain. We still need our own run.

source: d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro (2026, ACL Findings) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv v2, Apr 2026)
finding: Over 1M annotated reasoning traces, spontaneous mid-trace 'wait, actually' shifts are rare and go with lower accuracy, so they are not intrinsic self-correction. But adding a reconsideration cue in a second pass raised accuracy on math, and more so when the first pass had high token entropy. This is a gated re-ask, the same shape as Cao's retry, but with a token-level signal.
numbers: Pooled shifts 6.31% of traces; accuracy 2.57% with a shift vs 16.44% without (N=723,200, Qwen2.5-1.5B runs). Formal 'Aha' events 1.79%. GPT-4o shift rate 0.88% to 2.21%; DeepSeek-R1 0.00% to 0.25%. Forced reconsideration, Math, paired N=320,000: 0.3221 -> 0.4062 (+8.41 pp), 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong; Xwords +0.45 pp (5,380 vs 5,004). A 500-problem follow-up with cue variants: Qwen2.5-7B +5.97 pp, Llama 3.1-8B -4.19 pp.
quote: mid-reasoning shifts are symptoms of unstable inference behavior
limits: Small models (1.5B to 8B), GRPO-tuned on narrow tasks, plus GPT-4o and R1 only for shift counts. Pass 2 is compared to Pass 1, and I did not find a plain re-ask arm without the cue in the tables I read, so part of the +8.41 may be resampling plus regression to the mean. The sign flips across models (+5.97 vs -4.19).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: shows the placebo is the missing arm, not that the gain is fake. Gap 7: for reasoning models, spontaneous correction is not what helps; an externally triggered second look, gated on uncertainty, can.

source: Nguyen, Gupta, Le (2026) Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Adaptive Test-Time Reasoning (UAB, arXiv v2 Oct 2026)
finding: A matched-budget test of adaptive sample allocation against plain self-consistency, with three seeds and a paired bootstrap. Every question gets 2 probe samples; the rest of a fixed total budget goes to questions whose probes disagree. The total budget is met exactly. It beats uniform self-consistency, but the gain shrinks as budget grows, and a simpler adaptive early-stopping rule (ASC) is as good or better for the two large models.
numbers: Budget N=4 samples per question on average. Qwen2.5-1.5B average over 5 benchmarks: single call 40.4, Random 43.1, Uniform SC 45.0, ASC 45.2, UAB 47.0. Llama3.2-3B: Uniform 45.5, ASC 47.0, UAB 47.9. UAB beats Uniform in 14 of 15 settings, average +2.5, up to +5.5 on GSM8K; paired bootstrap significant (p<0.05) in 9 of 15. GPT-OSS-20B +2.7 and Gemma3-27B +1.5 over Uniform, but ASC edges UAB on both. In Table 8 the MATH500 rows show +1.8 (p=0.00) at N=4 falling to +0.5 (p=0.42) at N=16. Three seeds (42, 44, 46), temperature 1, 1,024 max new tokens.
limits: Small and mid open models, short outputs, answer-agreement signal only. No frontier reasoning model, no retry with feedback, no confidence elicited from the model.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 3 partly closed in one regime: allocating by agreement at equal total samples gives +1.5 to +2.7 over uniform voting, mostly at low budget. That is far below the harness headline (+8.6), and the gain is not guaranteed at large N or for strong models.

source: Nguyen, Gupta, Le (2026) UAB, signal ablation (Table 4, Appendix F)
finding: A same-model, same-budget comparison of difficulty signals for allocation, including logprob signals. Sample disagreement (vote entropy from 2 probes) had the best AUROC and the best accuracy, ahead of one-sample logprob signals.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B, N=4, average accuracy and AUROC against correctness: NLL 44.4 / 0.742; Token variance 44.8 / 0.672; Max token NLL 45.0 / 0.688; ANLL 44.9 / 0.662; Vote entropy (K=2) 47.0 / 0.780. 'Allocation alone accounts for at least half of UAB's gain over Uniform.'
limits: The vote-entropy arm uses one extra sample (K=2 vs K=1 for logprob signals), as the authors state. Small model; math and logic tasks. No verbalized-confidence arm.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly closed for black-box use: agreement across two samples beats single-sample logprob signals and needs no logprobs. It was not compared with verbalized JOL or a verifier in this paper.

source: Zhai, Li, Xiao, Li, Wang (2026) Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation for Reasoning LLMs via Constrained Policy Optimization
finding: A direct matched-average-budget test of directed against random allocation. A gradient-boosted classifier on 16 cheap text features (including one entropy estimate) assigns a sampling budget per question. At the same or lower mean cost it beats a random allocation with the same expected budget, by 3 to 4 points on MATH.
numbers: MATH, 200 questions, mean of 3 classifier seeds, B in {1.5, 2.0, 3.0}. DeepSeek-V3: Random 0.519 / 0.517 / 0.534 vs learned 0.550 / 0.562 / 0.575 (costs 1.45 / 1.87 / 2.73, below the random arm's 1.49 / 2.00 / 2.98); oracle 0.555 / 0.571 / 0.586. GPT-4o-mini B=3.0: random 0.487 vs learned 0.526. Qwen2.5-7B B=3.0: random 0.515 vs learned 0.554. GSM8K (94.6% base): 0.946 -> 0.965.
limits: N=200 per dataset; the plus-minus values are across classifier seeds with a fixed question set, not question-level CIs (a std of .001 cannot be a sampling CI). Oracle labels come from the same 48-sample pool as the test. Math only, majority voting only.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 evidence for directed over random at matched budget: +3 to +4 points, larger than Cao's 1.3, on N=200. The signal is cheap text features, not metacognitive confidence. So directed allocation is real for sampling; it says nothing yet about retry with feedback.

source: Del, Kangsepp, Domnich, Tampuu, Yankovskaya, Kull, Fishel (2026) How Uncertainty Estimation Scales with Sampling in Reasoning Models
finding: Black-box confidence from three open reasoning models (gpt-oss-20b, Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B) on 17 tasks. A single verbalized confidence (VC) is a strong baseline; self-consistency (SC) starts lower and does not overtake VC up to 8 samples. Combining the two with just 2 samples beats either signal at 8 samples.
numbers: Math: VC AUROC 71.3 at K=1 -> 81.4 at K=8; SC at K=2 70.5 (math), 66.6 (STEM), 63.3 (humanities); combined SCVC at K=2 84.2 in math (+12.9 over VC@1), +6.4 in STEM and humanities. A matched-token check with gpt-oss-20b: SC is weaker under extended reasoning than under shallow reasoning. 10 samples per question, up to 60K tokens each, bootstrap CIs.
limits: Open models of 8B to 30B size, not Claude. AUROC against correctness, not an end-to-end stop-or-retry accuracy test.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 largely answered for reasoning models without logprobs: verbalized confidence plus one extra sample of agreement is the best cost trade. Supports Cao's verbalized JOL, and suggests adding a second sample's agreement to the controller input.

source: Zollo, Wang, Zemel (2026) Binary Agreement for Efficient Unsupervised Confidence Calibration of Reasoning LLMs (BASC, arXiv v2 Oct 2026)
finding: Across 9 reasoning models (Qwen, DeepSeek, Nemotron) and 36 model-dataset pairs, raw single-sample verbalized confidence is badly calibrated and weakly discriminative, while test-time self-consistency is good. Label-free recalibration with two samples per training query closes most of the calibration gap.
numbers: Averages over 36 combinations: verbalized confidence ECE 0.268, Brier 0.281, AUROC 0.635; token probabilities ECE 0.197, AUROC 0.655; BASC-L (k=2) ECE 0.083, AUROC 0.685; test-time self-consistency ECE 0.090, AUROC 0.836; supervised recalibration ECE 0.051, AUROC 0.732. VC ECE by task: math 0.135, QA 0.401.
limits: Open reasoning models; the verbalized-confidence AUROC here (0.635) is much lower than Cao's Sonnet JOL (0.745), so model and prompt matter a lot. Not Claude.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: on most reasoning models, raw verbalized confidence fails the ECE < 0.15 bar and sits near the AUROC 0.6 bar. Recalibration is required. Two-sample agreement is an alternative to a labelled anchor set.

source: Sharma and Chopra (2025) The Sequential Edge: Inverse-Entropy Voting Beats Parallel Self-Consistency at Matched Compute
finding: At a matched token budget, sequential chains that see the full previous reasoning beat parallel independent chains in 43 of 45 configurations on AIME and GPQA-Diamond. This points the opposite way from Cao's context ablation (full previous context 40.0 below independent sampling 45.0).
numbers: 5 open models, 3, 6, 9 chains; each step capped at 4,096 tokens, 6 chains = 24,576 tokens either way. Largest gap Qwen3-235B AIME-2025 6 chains: sequential 76.7 vs parallel 30.0. GPQA-Diamond gains 11 to 14.6. Single seed 42, temperature 0.7, about 30 problems per AIME year.
limits: My reading, not the authors': a 4,096-token cap per chain truncates long reasoning, so independent chains may be cut off while sequential chains can continue; that would inflate the sequential edge. Single seed, 30-problem sets, open models, math and science only.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open and now has a counter-result: whether prior reasoning helps or anchors depends on the per-attempt budget and on whether the prior attempt is a continuation or a retry. Test compact vs full vs none at equal tokens with uncapped reasoning.

source: DosSantos DiSorbo and Ju (2026) Act or Escalate? Evaluating Escalation Behavior in Automation with Language Models
finding: A decision-theory test of act versus escalate with explicit error costs, in recorded human decisions, on 8 models (Qwen3.5, GPT-5 nano and mini, Llama, Mistral). Implicit escalation thresholds differ widely between models and are not predicted by scale; self-estimated accuracy is miscalibrated in model-specific ways. Cost framing alone does nothing for small models but works with extended thinking.
numbers: Thresholds (accuracy at which the model escalates 50% of the time): Qwen3.5-9B 56% vs Qwen3.5-397B 81%; GPT-5-nano 91% vs GPT-5-mini 53%. Self-estimated accuracy 76% to 97% vs actual 75% to 80%. Qwen 9B cost-optimal decisions: 62.0% baseline, +1.9 with cost framing, -0.1 with thinking, 78.8% with both. GPT-5-mini: 64.7 base, 87.1 with reasoning plus cost framing. SFT on chain-of-thought targets is the most robust fix.
limits: One-step prediction and escalate decisions on recorded data, not multi-step agent rollouts with external feedback. Reasoning is toggled; no Claude model. Only 8 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly: with action costs, models do not hold a stable threshold. A code-level controller with a calibrated threshold should own the act/escalate cut, not the model's own stance.

source: Liu et al. (2026) AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act? (abstract page only)
finding: A benchmark of paired tasks, one to be done and one to be refused, in tool sandboxes with real action consequences. Abstaining is largely independent of solving, and agents often abstain too late, after an irreversible step.
numbers: 263 paired tasks, 42 sandbox environments, 17 frontier LLMs, 4 agent harnesses. The best model (Gemini 3.1 Pro) reaches 59.5% paired accuracy. Annotators rated 94% to 98% of sampled tasks well designed.
limits: Only the abstract page was read (the PDF download was rate limited), so per-model results, confidence use and prompt effects were not seen.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: shows the agent setting is hard for abstention and that post-hoc abstention exists. Our gate must sit before irreversible actions and be tested on a paired act/abstain design like this.

source: Ding (2026) When LLMs Agree, Are They Right? Auditing Self-Consistency and Cross-Model Agreement as Confidence Signals (arXiv v2 Jul 2026)
finding: A crowd study with 53 runners drawing K=50 samples on the same GPQA and AIME cases. Agreement predicts majority-vote correctness positively but weakly, and the link can break for a stronger model that is over-confident.
numbers: Spearman correlation of agreement C with majority-correct M is positive in all 12 cells, none above 0.6. gpt-4.1 vs mini on the same cases: (C, M) -0.18 [-0.31, -0.03] on GPQA and -0.26 [-0.40, -0.12] on AIME (a difference between the models); gpt-4.1 mean C 0.89, ECE 0.41 on GPQA, and 48% wrong [0.40, 0.56] when agreement is at least 0.8. Chain-of-thought mini: M +0.066 on GPQA (not significant) and +0.080 on AIME.
limits: gpt-4.1 family, non-reasoning, 2025 snapshots; runs by students with their own prompts; snapshots not logged. Not a stop-rule test.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 boundary: agreement-based stopping can approve confident wrong answers when samples share a bias. Use agreement as a gate only with a second signal (JOL or a verifier), as Del et al. suggest.
